rationale:
Split into two independent, reusable analytic facts that use different techniques. The parent is left with only the enumeration bookkeeping of its step 2.

(1) plateau_weak_limit (parent steps 1 and 3). For any reals p, q, one fixed sequence of C¹ plateaus χ_k = σ(k(·−p))σ(k(q−·)), σ = Real.smoothTransition, has tsupport ⊆ [p,q] and satisfies ∫ χ_k g → ∫_{(p,q)} g for every integrable g (smooth transition + dominated convergence).

(2) ae_zero_of_rat_intervals (parent steps 0, 4 and 5). A function integrable on (c,d) whose integral over every rational subinterval (p,q) vanishes is a.e. zero on (c,d) (continuous primitive + density of ℚ + Lebesgue differentiation via IsUnifLocDoublingMeasure.ae_tendsto_average).

How the children imply the selected statement, following the supplied proof:
- Choose χ_{p,q,k} from child 1 for all reals p, q.
- Take a surjection e : ℕ → ℚ×ℚ×ℕ (exists_surjective_nat; Countable ℚ is available in the import closure).
- Set F_n := χ_{p,q,k} if e(n) = (p,q,k) with c < p and q < d, and F_n := 0 otherwise.
- Each F_n is C¹, and tsupport F_n is either contained in [p,q] ⊆ (c,d) (Icc_subset_Ioo) or empty.
- Let w be integrable on (c,d) with ∫ F_n w = 0 for all n, and fix rationals c<p<q<d. Put w̄ = 1_{(c,d)}w, which is integrable. Then χ_{p,q,k}w̄ = χ_{p,q,k}w pointwise, because χ vanishes off [p,q] ⊆ (c,d). Hence ∫ χ_{p,q,k}w̄ = ∫ F_n w = 0 for all k.
- Child 1 gives ∫_{(p,q)} w̄ = lim 0 = 0 = ∫_{(p,q)} w, and child 2 then gives w = 0 a.e. on (c,d).
- The case d ≤ c needs no separate treatment.

subproblems.title: Smooth plateau functions converge weakly to the indicator of an interval
subproblems.statement: For all real numbers p, q there is a sequence (χ_k)_{k∈ℕ} of C¹ functions ℝ → ℝ with tsupport χ_k ⊆ [p, q] for every k, such that for every Lebesgue-integrable function g : ℝ → ℝ, ∫_ℝ χ_k(α)·g(α) dα → ∫_{(p,q)} g(α) dα as k → ∞.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ p q : ℝ, ∃ χ : ℕ → ℝ → ℝ, (∀ k, ContDiff ℝ 1 (χ k)) ∧ (∀ k, tsupport (χ k) ⊆ Icc p q) ∧ ∀ g : ℝ → ℝ, Integrable g → Tendsto (fun k => ∫ α, χ k α * g α) atTop (𝓝 (∫ α in Ioo p q, g α))
subproblems.natural_proof:
Role: this is steps 1 and 3 of the parent-supplied proof (smooth plateau functions and the dominated-convergence passage), stated for one fixed pair p, q and an arbitrary integrable g. No assumption p < q is needed.
1. (Smooth transition.) Let σ := Real.smoothTransition. It is C^∞ (Real.smoothTransition.contDiff), satisfies 0 ≤ σ(x) ≤ 1 for all x (Real.smoothTransition.nonneg, Real.smoothTransition.le_one), σ(x) = 0 for x ≤ 0 (Real.smoothTransition.zero_of_nonpos) and σ(x) = 1 for x ≥ 1 (Real.smoothTransition.one_of_one_le).
2. (Definition.) For k ∈ ℕ, regarded as a real number k ≥ 0, put χ_k(α) := σ(k(α − p))·σ(k(q − α)). We show that the sequence (χ_k) has the three required properties; the same sequence works for every g.
3. (C¹.) The maps α ↦ k(α − p) and α ↦ k(q − α) are affine, hence C^∞ (contDiff_const.mul (contDiff_id.sub contDiff_const), resp. contDiff_const.mul (contDiff_const.sub contDiff_id)). Composing with σ gives C¹ functions (ContDiff.comp), and their product χ_k is C¹ (ContDiff.mul). In particular χ_k is continuous. This proves the first conjunct.
4. (Vanishing off (p, q).) Let α ∉ (p, q); then α ≤ p or q ≤ α. If α ≤ p, then k(α − p) ≤ 0 (a product of k ≥ 0 and α − p ≤ 0), so σ(k(α − p)) = 0 and χ_k(α) = 0. If q ≤ α, then k(q − α) ≤ 0, so σ(k(q − α)) = 0 and χ_k(α) = 0. Hence support χ_k ⊆ (p, q) ⊆ [p, q]. Since [p, q] is closed, tsupport χ_k = closure(support χ_k) ⊆ [p, q] (closure_minimal, isClosed_Icc). This proves the second conjunct. (If q ≤ p, then χ_k ≡ 0 and tsupport χ_k = ∅.)
5. (Bound.) For all k and α, 0 ≤ χ_k(α) ≤ 1·1 = 1, a product of two numbers in [0, 1]. Hence |χ_k(α)·g(α)| ≤ |g(α)| for every function g and every α.
6. (Pointwise limit.) Let g : ℝ → ℝ be any function and fix α. If p < α < q, then α − p > 0 and q − α > 0; choose N ∈ ℕ with N ≥ max(1/(α − p), 1/(q − α)) (exists_nat_ge). For k ≥ N we get k(α − p) ≥ (1/(α − p))(α − p) = 1 and likewise k(q − α) ≥ 1, so χ_k(α) = 1·1 = 1 and χ_k(α)g(α) = g(α) = 1_{(p,q)}(α)g(α) for all k ≥ N. If α ∉ (p, q), then by step 4, χ_k(α)g(α) = 0 = 1_{(p,q)}(α)g(α) for all k. In both cases χ_k(α)g(α) → (1_{(p,q)}·g)(α) as k → ∞, where 1_{(p,q)}·g is the function equal to g on (p, q) and to 0 elsewhere (Set.indicator).
7. (Dominated convergence.) Now let g be integrable. Each χ_k·g is a.e.-strongly measurable (χ_k is continuous and g is a.e.-strongly measurable, being integrable); |χ_k·g| ≤ |g| everywhere (step 5) and |g| is integrable; and χ_k·g → 1_{(p,q)}·g at every point (step 6). By the dominated convergence theorem (tendsto_integral_of_dominated_convergence with bound |g|), ∫_ℝ χ_k(α)g(α) dα → ∫_ℝ (1_{(p,q)}·g)(α) dα as k → ∞. Since (p, q) is measurable, ∫_ℝ 1_{(p,q)}·g = ∫_{(p,q)} g (integral_indicator, measurableSet_Ioo). This proves the third conjunct. ∎
proof_key_steps: Define χ_k(α) = σ(k(α−p))·σ(k(q−α)) with σ = Real.smoothTransition; it is C¹ as a product of compositions of σ with affine maps.
If α ≤ p or α ≥ q one argument of σ is ≤ 0, so χ_k vanishes off (p,q) and tsupport χ_k ⊆ [p,q] by closure_minimal.
For p<α<q, χ_k(α) = 1 once k ≥ max(1/(α−p), 1/(q−α)); otherwise χ_k(α) = 0; so χ_k g → 1_{(p,q)} g pointwise.
Dominated convergence with bound |g| and integral_indicator give ∫ χ_k g → ∫_{(p,q)} g for every integrable g.

subproblems.title: Vanishing integrals over all rational subintervals force a.e. vanishing
subproblems.statement: Let c, d be real numbers and let w : ℝ → ℝ be Lebesgue-integrable on (c, d). If ∫_{(p,q)} w(α) dα = 0 for all rational numbers p, q with c < p < q < d, then w vanishes almost everywhere on (c, d): for almost every α ∈ ℝ, α ∈ (c, d) implies w(α) = 0.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (c d : ℝ) (w : ℝ → ℝ), IntegrableOn w (Ioo c d) → (∀ p q : ℚ, c < (p : ℝ) → (p : ℝ) < (q : ℝ) → (q : ℝ) < d → ∫ α in Ioo (p : ℝ) (q : ℝ), w α = 0) → ∀ᵐ α, α ∈ Ioo c d → w α = 0
subproblems.natural_proof:
Role: this is steps 0, 4 and 5 of the parent-supplied proof (primitive and Lebesgue differentiation); the conclusion of the parent's step 3 (vanishing integrals over rational subintervals) is taken as the hypothesis.
0. (Empty interval.) If d ≤ c, then (c, d) = ∅, so for every α the implication α ∈ (c, d) → w(α) = 0 holds vacuously, and the a.e. statement follows. Assume c < d from now on and write J := (c, d).
1. (Extension by zero.) Let w̄ := 1_J·w (Set.indicator: w̄ = w on J, w̄ = 0 off J). Since w is integrable on J and J is measurable, w̄ is integrable on ℝ (IntegrableOn.integrable_indicator). If p, q are rationals with c < p < q < d, then (p, q) ⊆ J, so w̄ = w on (p, q) and ∫_{(p,q)} w̄ = ∫_{(p,q)} w = 0 by hypothesis (setIntegral_congr_fun).
2. (Primitive.) Let W(x) := ∫_c^x w̄ (interval integral). Since w̄ is integrable on ℝ, it is interval-integrable on every interval (Integrable.intervalIntegrable), so W is continuous on ℝ (intervalIntegral.continuous_primitive) and W(b) − W(a) = ∫_a^b w̄ for all real a, b (intervalIntegral.integral_interval_sub_left). For rationals c < p < q < d:
   W(q) − W(p) = ∫_p^q w̄ = ∫_{(p,q]} w̄ = ∫_{(p,q)} w̄ = 0
   (intervalIntegral.integral_of_le since p ≤ q; integral_Ioc_eq_integral_Ioo since points are Lebesgue-null; step 1). Hence W(q) = W(p).
3. (W vanishes on [c, d].) Fix a rational q₀ with c < q₀ < d (exists_rat_btwn, using c < d). For every rational r with c < r < d we have W(r) = W(q₀): if r < q₀ apply step 2 to the pair (r, q₀); if q₀ < r apply it to (q₀, r); if r = q₀ there is nothing to prove. Let S := J ∩ ℚ (rationals regarded as reals). Then S ⊆ J ⊆ [c, d]. Moreover [c, d] ⊆ closure S: the rationals are dense in ℝ (Rat.denseRange_cast) and J is open, so J ⊆ closure(J ∩ ℚ) = closure S (Dense.open_subset_closure_inter); hence closure J ⊆ closure S (closure_minimal, closure S being closed), and closure J = [c, d] because c ≠ d (closure_Ioo). The continuous function W and the constant function with value W(q₀) agree on S, so they agree on [c, d] (Set.EqOn.of_subset_closure, ℝ being Hausdorff). In particular, since c ∈ [c, d], W(q₀) = W(c) = ∫_c^c w̄ = 0 (intervalIntegral.integral_same). Therefore W(x) = 0 for every x ∈ [c, d].
4. (Lebesgue differentiation.) Lebesgue measure on ℝ is uniformly locally doubling (instance IsUnifLocDoublingMeasure volume, via MeasureTheory.Measure.isUnifLocDoublingMeasureOfIsAddHaarMeasure), ℝ is a second-countable Borel space, volume is locally finite, and w̄ is locally integrable because it is integrable (Integrable.locallyIntegrable). By IsUnifLocDoublingMeasure.ae_tendsto_average applied to w̄ with K = 1, for almost every x ∈ ℝ the following holds: for every filter l on an index type ι and all maps y : ι → ℝ, δ : ι → ℝ such that δ → 0 within (0, ∞) along l and eventually x ∈ closedBall(y_j, 1·δ_j), the averages ⨍_{closedBall(y_j, δ_j)} w̄ converge to w̄(x) along l. Fix such a point x and assume x ∈ J (the remaining points satisfy the target implication trivially). Take ι := ℝ, l := 𝓝[>] 0, y_ρ := x and δ_ρ := ρ. Then δ → 0 within (0, ∞) (tendsto_id), and for every ρ > 0, which holds eventually in 𝓝[>] 0 (self_mem_nhdsWithin), x ∈ closedBall(x, 1·ρ) (mem_closedBall_self, as 1·ρ ≥ 0). Hence ⨍_{closedBall(x, ρ)} w̄ → w̄(x) as ρ → 0⁺.
5. (The averages vanish.) Put m := min(x − c, d − x); m > 0 since c < x < d. Let 0 < ρ < m. Then closedBall(x, ρ) = [x − ρ, x + ρ] (Real.closedBall_eq_Icc), and c ≤ x − ρ ≤ x + ρ ≤ d, so x − ρ and x + ρ lie in [c, d]. Therefore
   ∫_{[x−ρ, x+ρ]} w̄ = ∫_{(x−ρ, x+ρ]} w̄ = ∫_{x−ρ}^{x+ρ} w̄ = W(x + ρ) − W(x − ρ) = 0 − 0 = 0
   (integral_Icc_eq_integral_Ioc; intervalIntegral.integral_of_le since x − ρ ≤ x + ρ; step 2; step 3). Consequently ⨍_{closedBall(x, ρ)} w̄ = (vol[x − ρ, x + ρ])⁻¹ · 0 = 0 (setAverage_eq). Since (0, m) ∈ 𝓝[>] 0 (Ioo_mem_nhdsGT), the averages are eventually equal to 0 along 𝓝[>] 0, so they converge to 0 (tendsto_const_nhds.congr'). As 𝓝[>] 0 is a nontrivial filter on ℝ, uniqueness of limits (tendsto_nhds_unique) together with step 4 gives w̄(x) = 0.
6. (Conclusion.) Since x ∈ J, w(x) = w̄(x) = 0 (Set.indicator_of_mem). Steps 4–5 apply to almost every x ∈ ℝ, so for almost every x ∈ ℝ, x ∈ (c, d) implies w(x) = 0, which is the claim. ∎
proof_key_steps: If d ≤ c the claim is vacuous; otherwise extend w by zero to the integrable w̄ = 1_J·w, whose integral over each rational (p,q) ⊆ (c,d) is 0.
The primitive W(x) = ∫_c^x w̄ is continuous and W(q) = W(p) for all rationals c<p<q<d.
W agrees with the constant W(q₀) on ℚ∩(c,d), which is dense in [c,d]; hence W ≡ W(c) = 0 on [c,d].
Lebesgue differentiation (IsUnifLocDoublingMeasure.ae_tendsto_average, K = 1, centre x, radius ρ → 0⁺) gives ⨍_{closedBall x ρ} w̄ → w̄(x) for a.e. x.
For x ∈ (c,d) and 0<ρ<min(x−c,d−x), ∫_{[x−ρ,x+ρ]} w̄ = W(x+ρ) − W(x−ρ) = 0, so the averages vanish eventually and w(x) = w̄(x) = 0.
